title: SYSK Selects: Did Reagan's Star Wars program win the Cold War?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (originally released August 2012) of "Did Reagan's Star Wars program win the Cold War?" Josh introduces the episode, then the hosts discuss mutual assured destruction and Reagan's March 1983 call to make nuclear weapons "impotent and obsolete," which led to the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), nicknamed "Star Wars" by the press. They cover Soviet opposition and the ABM and Outer Space treaties, the Fletcher Report, the Reykjavik talks with Gorbachev where Soviet demands were tied to giving up SDI, the Soviet response, and whether the program helped end the Cold War. Technologies discussed include Edward Teller's X-ray laser (Project Excalibur), kinetic warheads, rail guns, the MIRACL laser, and the "bright pebbles" space-based interceptors. The episode also covers SDI's continuation under George H. W. Bush and Clinton, its influence on today's missile defense, and a closing listener mail segment.
rerun_of: Did Reagan's Star Wars program win the Cold War?

segments.title: Rerun intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the SYSK Selects rerun of the August 2012 episode. The hosts exchange banter, then Josh addresses newcomers about the show not claiming to be experts.

segments.title: Mutual assured destruction and Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative
segments.summary: The hosts describe mutual assured destruction as the Cold War standoff and Reagan's March 1983 address calling for nuclear weapons to be made impotent and obsolete. This led to the Strategic Defense Initiative, dubbed Star Wars by the press, which the Soviets and many Americans opposed.

segments.title: Treaties, Congress, and the Star Wars name
segments.summary: The Soviets argued SDI violated the ABM Treaty and the Outer Space Treaty. Ted Kennedy reportedly coined the term Star Wars, and Reagan tried unsuccessfully to get the name dropped in favor of Strategic Defense Initiative. European allies and Congress had concerns about cost and feasibility.

segments.title: Fletcher Report and Reykjavik summit
segments.summary: The Fletcher Report listed technologies needed for SDI. Reagan treated SDI as a possible bargaining chip. At the Reykjavik summit in Iceland, Gorbachev reportedly offered arms reductions contingent on giving up SDI, and Reagan walked out.

segments.title: Soviet response and the fall of the Soviet Union
segments.summary: The Soviets launched a counter program to defeat SDI but lacked funding. The hosts argue the program added financial pressure on the Soviet Union, which collapsed within less than a decade of the initiative's announcement, and note the US covert role in Afghanistan.

segments.title: Bush and Clinton scale back SDI
segments.summary: After the Soviet fall, George H. W. Bush refocused and cut back SDI, and Clinton refined and reduced it further, so it was far from Reagan's original plan.

segments.title: Space-based weapons concepts: X-ray lasers, kinetic warheads, rail guns, bright pebbles
segments.summary: The hosts describe proposed SDI technologies: Edward Teller's nuclear-powered X-ray laser (Project Excalibur), which failed and drew ridicule and accusations of falsified tests; kinetic warheads from a satellite garage; rail guns; the MIRACL ground-based laser; and bright pebbles, thousands of small autonomous interceptors that would have been cheap and were partly tested via the Clementine probe.

segments.title: Legacy of SDI and missile defense
segments.summary: Some SDI tests succeeded, and the hosts say its sensor and missile defense research influenced today's ballistic missile defense system, including a recent test interception over the Pacific.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts read listener questions about their recording seats, favorite Marvel hero, favorite band, coffee preferences, and favorite foods, then sign off.
